Mr. D. .1. COWAN (Port Arthur-Thunder Bay):	Mr. Speaker, the bill now 'before the
house has been too long delayed. I think it would have been in the interests of the war veterans themselves and of the public generally if this legislation had' been introduced some years ago. It would have come with a much better grace if it had come spontaneously from the hearts of the Canadian people as expressed here, rather than being forced through the agency of the legion from a most reluctant government.
In common with other members who have spoken this afternoon, I adhere to the principle of support or aid or recompense for the returned soldiers of this country. They left our Shores with loud hurrahs ringing in their ears and with the implied promise that upon their return they would be reestablished in civil life, or if they did not return that their dependents would be adequately oared for. This proposed legislation does not meet the full requirements of the legion in my community with which I have the honour to be connected in an honorary capacity, in that

it is deficient in providing for the relief of our returned men, for various reasons, of which I will state a few.
First, in the definition clause the word "veteran" is not sufficiently inclusive. I know that this and other deficiencies will be .considered in the special committee to which this bill will be referred, and I sincerely hope the government will give earnest consideration to these deficiencies so that when itihe bill is reported they will be remedied. The word "veteran," as I say, is not sufficiently inclusive, for it does not cover those veterans who served in Canada and in England. The definition should be so widened as to include those veterans. In the second place, no benefit is provided for dependents. I think the proper course would be to amend the Pension Act so that the dependents of these men could be properly provided for. In the third' place, the clause in regard to disallowance is too strict. If a war veteran has conveyed his property within five years of the time of his application, the conveyance is deemed to have been made for the purpose of getting the allowance under this bill. I submit that a great many of these men have had to dispose of their property during that period, that they have been forced to do so iby the pansimony of this government in looking after them, and that it is most unfair and unjust that a man who by reason of those circumstances has had to dispose of his property should be debarred from the benefits of this bill.

Mr. Speaker, may I interrupt the hon. gentleman for a moment?
I am afraid my hon. friend has not read very carefully the provisions of the bill. The disallowance applies if the man sells his property after the coming into force of this proposed legislation,

Even so it seems to me [DOT]
unwise that any one coming within the terms of this bill should be debarred by reason of having disposed of his property in the subsequent five years.
That is quite true.

He should be entitled to
the benefits of this bill even if he has to dispose of his property within the next five years. Then the age limit is too high. A great number of our men who went overseas would not be entitled to the benefits of this legislation until forty years had elapsed from the beginning of hostilities. That in itself is an unwise position for the government to take, because I think that on the average our men enlisted at twenty-five years of age, and I sub-

Allowances to War Veterans
mit they should not have to wait until they are sixty-five until they come under the benefits of this legislation; it is too long a time altogether for them to have to wait.
I was amazed this afternoon to learn of the expense of administering the Pension Act. When you find that the cost of its administration so far as appeals are concerned was greater than the benefits which have been awarded to our returned men, I think the uselessness and futility of setting up another commission to administer this proposed legislation is apparent.

Mr. Speaker, I
must take exception to that statement. A similar statement was made earlier this afternoon, but it is not borne out by the facts. I hope to speak on that in the course of the evening.

For the moment I accept
the correction of the minister. I am relying on the statement to that effect, made, I think, by the member for North York (Mr. Lennox).
He is in error.

But undoubtedly the expenses of administration are out of all proportion to the benefits received. If the commission which will administer this proposed legislation is going to follow along the same lines, then I submit that one of two things will happen: either the cost of administration will be altogether too high, or the benefits awarded will be entirely lacking in generosity. I take this further objection that the allowance granted to a man is suspended while he is undergoing hospital treatment. May I point out that that is the very time when his allowance should go on, because many of our returned men have not saved up anything for the proverbial rainy day. It seems to me that as necessarily their wages cease while they are receiving hospital treatment, they should be afforded an opportunity of obtaining the benefits of this legislation during that time.
I subscribe to the principle that aid should be given to our veterans. Of course, it is better, as in this case, to get half a loaf than none. The bill is good as far as it goes, but the allowance is too small, and I think the condition of the ex^soldier has not been properly or sympathetically treated in this bill. For these reasons, therefore, Mr. Speaker, I sincerely hope that the government will reconsider its attitude and show greater generosity to the men who did so much for us in the days that are past. [DOT]

Mr. Speaker, when the minister introduced the bill 1 understood him to say that it was all the legislation which he intended bringing down this session in connection with pension matters. That statement, to me, was most amazing and disappointing. I think that further amendments to the Pension Act are due, in fact now considerably overdue-

And are being
considered now by a committee.

At any rate be that as
it may be, in my opinion this bill does not go far enough. The executive representatives of the Canadian Legion in my county have to-day, I am advised, forty-one cases before the pension board. Some of them have been before the board for a very considerable time; some that I know of and am personally interested in have been before the board for well on three years. I have in mind at the moment a case Which is well known to my hon. friend from Yukon (Mr. Black). It is that of a man who served under him in France, and has been repeatedly before the board. The man has been down at the military hospital in Halifax, and the doctors there who examined him stated that a certain condition as suggested by his own physician could not be present. Subsequently the man underwent an abdominal operation which disclosed that the very condition suggested by his own physician actually existed. Notwithstanding that, nothing has yet been done in regard to the case, although representations have been made, and repeatedly made, both by the member for Yukon and myself in regard to the matter.
Made to whom?

Made first to one doctor and then to another of the pension board. We as yet have obtained no redress. There is the case of a man who is not a malingerer. I I have known him intimately since he returned from the war. His wife is putting up a splendid fight to maintain a home and nurse her husband; fortunately for him she is a trained nurse. The man is not able to work. He has attempted to do so again and again, but after two or three days' work he breaks down and has to go back to the hospital. He has been nursed by a devoted wife over a period of half a dozen years. Conditions of that kind arouse resentment in all the friends of the soldiers who know the circumstances, as I know them in this particular case. But that is not the only one. I have in mind the case of a man named Mackay from Thorburn, also in my county, in which the circumstances are much the same. Now we are told that he can

Allowances to War Veterans
have a board some time in the near future, but we cannot get any definite information as to when he will go before the board. I have another case which is worse than either of those referred to, the case of Private Ernest Cameron, regimental No. 716171. He is suffering from a head wound. To-day he is a pauper patient in the harmless insane asylum in my home county. That man has a family, a wife and three children, now dependent entirely on charity. Why are cases of that kind not dealt with? It is not sufficient for the minister to say that this is all the legislation he proposes this year.

I think my hon. friend is hardly fair. The matter was made very plain the other night. I then said that this was the legislation the government presented to parliament at this time, a veterans' allowance act, that other returned soldier matters would be referred to a special committee of this house, and that suggested legislation would undoubtedly grow out of that committee and be again before the house.

But none is to
be brought down by the government?
It will be brought down by the government-it must be: it cannot be brought down otherwise. So there is no use labouring the point.

All I can say is and I
assert that the explanation of the minister is not in accordance with my understanding of what he distinctly stated. When he was asked from this side of the house if this was all the legislation he proposed to bring down, he said yes. Is not that correct?
You misunderstood entirely.

We are all liable to be misunderstood. But I want to tell the minister that my understanding of what he said and his understanding of it are quite different and the record, which I cannot at the moment put my hand on, will support my position. Further, as I said a few moments ago, if the minister has any such idea it certainly will not meet the case. That is not my view alone, it is the view of thousands of others in this country.
I have no intention further to discuss the matter except again to emphasize the fact that I have in my county a great number of cases relief for whom is long overdue and which demand more sympathetic consideration by a pension board with less restrictive regulations. As I stated on a former occasion when dealing with this matter, I have no 
quarrel with the pension board, from whom I have on many occasions received every courtesy in connection with cases that I have brought to their notice. The difficulty is they are hedged about with restrictions which do not permit them, in their judgment, to do what I consider simple elementary justice to many cases of the type that I have referred to to-night. Such restrictions must be swept away and replaced by a more humane and just enlargement'of the present Pension Act, now long overdue.

I should like t.o read one section of a letter that I received this afternoon. It is dated March 18, and reads as follows:
In further reference to the McGibbon resolution and Bill No. 19 I may say that I had occasion to attend the Glace Bay branch of the Canadian Legion on the occasion of their regular meeting last Sunday when this matter was discussed. Considerable indignation was expressed concerning Bill No. 19 and the meeting seemed to be in hearty accord with the resolution. At all events the branch decided to express their approval of the resolution and their disapproval of the bill and to submit the question to the provincial command from whence it will undoubtedly be forwarded for final decision to the Dominion command. The general impression is that the findings and submissions of the Regina convention this year are rather compatible with the resolution than with Bill No. 19. I agree with you that both bill and resolution might well be adopted for reasons stated in your letter of the 15th instant. In my opinion the Dominion command will support the resolution and find that it might be supplemented by Bill No. 19, but I feel quite confident that the bill alone will be unacceptable.
I may say that these ibwo councils are composed of clergymen, .miners, lawyers, labourers, doctors and men of all classes, and I think they compare in point of intelligence with any .council of the legion in any .part of the country. It is 'because they have conveyed to me in such distinct terms their disapproval of this bill that I feel it necessary at this stage to record my protest against it.

Mr.Speaker, I think the bill before the house should commend itself to us in a great many ways, and even if it does not go quite as far as we might wish, still I think it will bring relief to a certain number of men and will help meet the difficulty which now exists and with which we are all familiar.
Different speakers have referred to the present Pension Act, and it has been suggested that no amendment will be brought in this session. I am sure the comimitte which will consider soldier .problems will inquire into the different aspects of the question, and I feel sure .that i;f they bring in a strong recommendation to this house asking for amendments which can be accepted by the house, those recommendations will receive consideration and the necesary amendments will be brought in. At present we are considering Bill No. 19, which is entitled "An Aot Respecting War Veterans' Allowances," under which we intend to relieve a certain number of cases. In my opinion the cases at present which are the most difficult to deal with are those in which the present disability is due to over-

seas service, but in which the connection cannot be traced. In my experience in dealing with these cases I find that in the greater number, lung trouble, throat trouble, bronchial troulble or heart trouble has developed since the soldier was discharged, but that there is no way of proving that the disability is due to overseas service. If I understand this measure correctly, if these men are not able to carry on gainful employment they will receive an allowance. In addition there is the man who is at present in receipt of a small pension o<f from 5 .per cent to 14 .per cent. His case also will be considered and if he is not in a position to earn a livelihood he will come under the provisions of this act and receive some compensation.
However, there are certain people who will not receive any assistance under this act; I refer to the dependents of returned men. Under the present Pension Act a great many dependents do not receive any assistance. If I remember rightly, the dependents of a man who has been in receipt of a 75 per cent to 80 per cent pension receive consideration should that man die, but if the man is in receipt of a pension lower than that percentage no assistance will be given his dependents.
We hear a great deal, and often read in the newspapers, that the pension board should give compassionate consideration to these cases. I think that is hardly fair to the board, Mr. Speaker, because I believe no such thing as a compassionate consideration is possible. If the pension board can bring a case within the four comers of the Pension Act, I think it is agreed that usually they have done so and granted a pension, but they cannot consider a case from a compassionate point of view. Under the present act, they cannot go outside the strict limitations imposed upon them.
Why not amend the act?

That is what I am saying. In my opinion we should seek to bring in some amendment at this session whereby cases with which the pension board cannot deal under the present act will be taken care of if they are not provided for in the bill now before the house.
I think everyone is quite willing to give all the assistance possible in an endeavour of this kind. I do not think we should make political capital out of this matter; I think we should unite our efforts to make some improvements to the act in order to get the best results from legislation of this kind. We know that- in a number of cases the men are asked to produce medical certificates, and those certificates must date back to 1920 or 192? in order to be effective. Ir a great

Allowances to War Veterans
many cases men are not able to produce such medical certificates. A man may have received treatment before that time, but it may be that the doctor who attended him is not now alive. That man cannot produce a certificate, and under the act as it stands now he is deprived of pension.
It has been suggested that the onus of proof should be on the board. That is a debatable question. We have been told that the cost of administering the act at present is very high, and if the board had to go all over the country to get evidence of this kind it might be a very costly experiment. It might be far better so to amend the act-that cases such as we have referred to can be brought under the regulations. I sincerely hope that when the act is before the committee, every phase of these questions will be considered, together with the individual cases which have been referred to from time to time by different members of this house. I do not think it is quite fair to the pension board for us to get up in this house and cite certain cases which we think have not received proper consideration. There may be facts contained in the man's file of which we have no knowledge, so that when we discuss these matters, we may not have all the information. I feel that the pension board has given very careful consideration to the cases which have been brought before it, and I know that in every case where they can give any relief, they do so. However, in many instances it is impossible for them to do anything, and it is up to us to remedy that situation.
I am fully in accord with the principles of this bill, and if we can improve it when it goes to committee, well and good. If not, at least we are getting something for the returned men, and when the committee sits we should bend our efforts to securing further improvement if it is possible to do so.

'Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to observe the unanimity of opinion which seems to prevail in this house that the fullest measure of justice should be done to the returned man, and I think that is the feeling of the people at large of this Dominion. I have made several trips to the department and I must say that I have always met with very kind and courteous treatment from those who are in charge of the Pension Act, but I suppose that every hon. member of this house has gone to the board only to find that because of the difficulty in connecting a soldier's present disability with his services overseas no assistance could be obtained.
I have in mind the case of a young man who was too young to enlist when the war 2419-51
broke out. When he reached the required age he enlisted, went overseas, was seventeen months in the trenches, was wounded, had a severe attack of "flu " and other minor illnesses and was discharged in 1919. Before enlisting that man was perhaps the outstanding athlete in the community but upon his return he showed clearly the effect of the services which he had rendered to his country. He seemed to pick up a little but finally he took ill, gradually grew worse, and to-day that young man of only thirty-one years of age is in a pitiable condition. There is no possibility of his being any better and in all probability he will gradually grow worse, but due to an inability to connect up that man's present disabilities with his services overseas, no assistance can be obtained under the act as it now stands. It seems to me that such treatment is not the wish of the people of Canada. It may be said that this case will be taken care of under the bill which is being considered. But will it? Under the Pension Act we are met with the difficulty of connecting up his present disabilities with his services overseas, and I agree with the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Stinson) that similar difficulties will be met with under this bill unless we have a clear understanding of the term "permanently unemployable." Section 5 of the proposed bill reads:
(1) An allowance may be paid to every veteran who, at the date of the proposed commencement of the allowance,
(a) has attained the age of sixty-five years, or, not having attained the age of sixty years is, in the opinion of the committee, by reason of physical or mental disability, permanently unemployable;
I would like to know what "permanently unemployable" means. Will a man be considered ineligible who through disabilities is able to work, say one fifth of his time only? If that be so, then the case I have described, and similar cases, would be barred both under the Pension Act and under the provisions of this proposed bill. Before this bill receives its second reading I think we should have from the minister a clear definition of what is intended by that term.
There are other points in connection with this bill which I might mention, but they have been very well covered by other hon. members. I agree with the hon. members who have said they would prefer to see the Pension Act amended, and that wherever a doubt exists the benefit of that doubt should be given to the soldier. I would rather err on the side of leniency in the altering of the Pension Act and in the carrying out of the regulations than err in being too strict. Feeling



Allowances to War Veterans
as I do, Mr. Speaker, I would be prepared to go the limit in seeing that the fullest measure of justice is afforded to those men who answered the call of their country at a time when their services were so badly needed.

Mr. Speaker, I am in earnest sympathy with any phase of this bill which will provide relief to the ex-service man, but I would like to deal with the committee which is to administer this bill. We all know that the country was aroused by a letter written by General Currie which was read at the Regina convention of the legion. Following that letter, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) had the following to say:
So long as there is a sense of injustice among ex-service men it is the duty of the government to get rid of it.
He was reinforced by the remarks of the hon. Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) who said:
The duty of the people of Canada is not complete so long as there is one per cent of ex-service men to whom justice has not been done.
Then a later despatch from Ottawa quotes the Prime Minister as follows:
The Board of Pension Commissioners should regard itself as trustees of the rights and benefits extended to ex-service men and their dependents and not so much as trustees of the public funds.
The other day the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Smith) asked the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. King) if he would not suggest to the Board of Pension Commissioners that they give a little more generous interpretation to the act but he was informed that that could not be done.
There can be no justice given to the Canadian soldier so long as the government seeks to take political advantage of his disability and distress, and the government cannot do its duty to the returned man by putting the administration of this bill in the hands of the committee. Who will constitute that committee? It will consist of the Deputy Minister of Pensions, his assistant, and three to five other employees or officers of the department; and naturally the minister himself, being the head of the department. Who will say that the present Minister of Pensions and National Health is not weak enough to take political advantage of any benefits which might accrue from the provisions of this bill. We have in clause 5 for instance, the proposal that an allowance may be given to a veteran who is mentally and physically unable to obtain per-
manent employment. It does not say that it "shall", but that it "may". While the age limit of sixty-five is stated, discretion is left with the committee to say that a man under sixty years of age shall come within the benefits of the allowance. This discretion, as I say, is wholly with the committee or with the minister, which is precisely the same thing. No minister, on whichever side of politics he may be, should be clothed with such discretion and authority.
I should like to emphasize my reference to the present Minister of Pensions. He is my neighbour. The keenest interest he has is to defeat me, and I say with all frankness that my zeal is just as earnest to defeat him. I want to cite one or two little instances which, although they may be somewhat remote, indicate that a minister, and particularly the present one, should not be entrusted with such extensive discretion as is contained within this measure. The -minister was out in Vancouver last year and while addressing the Liberal Association he went on to say
That he wished to impress upon the people of V ancouver-
Not upon the Liberal Association 'but upon the -people of Vancouver.

that they had not acted politically in a fashion . which would influence government policies in their favour in the matter of trade.
In other words, he told the people of Vancouver that they had not returned enough government supporters.
To go back a little further, the minister and I happened ito be in the same campaign some ten years ago when the Mother's Pension Act was brought into force in British Columbia. He was a member of the administration and the bringing -into force of that act was somewhat delayed in order that the government might derive a little advantage from it by the distribution of cheques to the mothers just two -or -three weeks before the election. Those mothers' pension cheques, both in East Kootenay and in- West Kootenay, which is my constituency, were distributed by -the score. Who could expect any poor -woman to go out and hurrah for the Conservative party when the Liberal workers there were 'taking around the mothers' pension cheques?
I have another little instance in connection with the Vancouver Sun, which is certainly the most aggressive and pronounced Liberal organ in British Columbia. In August last the Vancouver Sun apparently recoignized the patronage tendencies of the Minister of Pensions, and it said that Liberal principles and policies have been used to keep Doctor King in office and his -friends in control of patron-

Allowances to War Veterans
age. Just think of placing in the hands of any single minister such responsibility as this bill involves. I do not wonder that the minister wants it, 'because it might help in a political way on the eve of an election. At the same time, no minister, regardless of party, should have such authority. An act like this should be administered by an independent commission or committee wholly divorced from political and departmental influence.	. .
Let me cite another instance. The Minister of Pensions came to Nelson, which is in my district, last September, I think it was, and he decried the fact that British Columbia was too much inclined to Conservatism. In other words he said: You are not sending enough Liberals to Ottawa. He said: "I am the only Liberal from British Columbia and I need help." Of course we all know he needs help-he will not need any after the next election. The point is that he emphasized that fact. He had a trifling meeting of, I think, about sixty people in Trail with a population of around 8,000. In fact he thanked me for having attended his meeting.
I told him I was going to follow him to Nelson to see whether he would change his tone and hoped he would do no more harm there than he did in Trail. What do you suppose he told them in Nelson? This remember is the man to whom we are going to entrust the administration of this great soldiers' allowance act. He said: "I am the minister from British Columbia, and nothing can be done without my recommendation." What is the result? The result is that any returned man under sixty years of age of the right political complexion if he secures the recommendation of the Minister of Pensions, might get this allowance; or we might put it in this way: perhaps the Liberal Association might suggest to the minister that he use his influence or, rather, give his consent that the allowance be given, and of course in that case the soldier would get it. I do not blame the minister for needing help; it is clear enough that he needs it. But what the returned man wants is his just due under the Pension Act.
No man can complain very much about the Board of Pension Commissioners; I have received every courtesy from them, but the trouble is that they are compelled to work under hard and fast rules and regulations. The government would have done much better and gone much further had it brought down, as it should have, amendments to the present Pension Act. There has been no specific statement either from the Prime Minister or from the Minister of Pensions that the Pension 2419-Sli
Act would be amended at this session. The other night the Minister of Pensions was asked specifically whether there would be any other legislation in connection with pensions, and he stated no. That statement appears specifically in Hansard.
There is another little incident which might be of interest. This is from the Prime Minister himself as far back as December 20. It is plain that at that time the intention of the government was to bring down amendments to the Pension Act, because the Prime Minister said under date of December 20:
Amendments to the Pension Act, with the object of giving more liberal treatment to ex-service men, will be introduced at the coming session of parliament.
That is a plain statement, but we have not seen any amendments yet.
Just what will be the nature of the amendments, the Prime Minister declined to indicate.
But he went on to say that they would be introduced into the house and would then be referred to a special committee. The returned men, and the people of Canada on behalf of the returned men, are looking for such amendments to the Pension Act as will do justice to the claims of those who served overseas, and I do hope that before this session ends such amendments will be brought down.

I feel
that this measure will not by any means give adequate relief to a very deserving class of people. It is intended to serve a very large class. There are many belonging to that class in the city and county from which I come who are suffering from disabilities presumably due to their war service, men still young or middleaged but who are showing all the symptoms of old age, and who being unable to find employment are now in destitute circumstances. For over ten years many of them have been suffering from disabilities, and now at this late date the government undertakes to grant them this very slight measure of relief, which is entirely inadequate for the purpose and does not do justice to a class so deserving.
The difficulty of the government is in recognizing that these disabilities are the result of war conditions. The Board of Pension Commissioners has interpreted the Pension Act in the case of these men in a very narrow way, and the proper tiling, I think, would be to amend the Pension Act so as to grant this particular class adequate relief. Instead of that, the government has seen fit to introduce a different measure entirely, which will by no means afford the relief to which this class is entitled. They are just

Allowances to War Veterans
as deserving as those who are now in receipt of Pensions under the Pension Act. They have given equal service; they have made the same sacrifice for the country's good; they are destitute, and I can see no reason why they should not receive from this country the same pension that is granted to pensioners under the schedules attached to the Pension Act. The government recognizes that they are suffering from disabilities caused by the war. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) himself, addressing the house a few days ago, said:
While there are many men to-day who are broken down as a result of strain during the period of war, they are unable to show that that impairment of their health is attributable to any specific cause connected with the war itself.
Again, he says:
The Pension Act does not meet the eases of those men who are breaking down to-day from causes undoubtedly due to service in a theatre of war-*
Note those words of the Prime Minister- "as a result of strain during the period of war," and "from causes undoubtedly due to service in a theatre of war." Why should not these men be put on the same footing as those who are receiving pensions under the Pension Act? Look at the measure of relief which they are to receive under this legislation? First, they must be of the age of sixty-five years. Many men who are suffering from disabilities now will not attain the age of sixty-five for twenty or twenty-five years, and until they reach that age they are to be without the small compensation offered by this leglislation unless they can satisfy the tribunal to be appointed by the government that they are permanently unemployable. I do not know just what those words mean. I thought that perhaps the bill would define them, but it does not do so. That has still to be defined, and unless a man can satisfy the tribunal that he is permanently unemployable he gets no compensation under this legislation until he reaches the age of sixty-five.
If he is eligible under this legislation, what does he receive? A pensioner under the Pension Act suffering from a permanent disability is entitled, if he is manned, to S125 a month. Under this legislation a married man receives only $40 a month, or $480 a year, and a single man only $20 a month or $240 a year. That is the most they can draw, and then only if their income is not more than $730 a year in the case of the married man, and $365 a year in the case of the single man. There is no reason why these men should be discriminated against in this way. They

should receive the same amount of compensation as the ordinary pensioner.
I take another exception to this bill, and that is as to the tribunal which is to investigate the claims. Pensions are dealt with by an independent board. Why should there be any difference made in this case? Why should the board be composed of officials of the department, entirely under the control of the minister? That is not a fair way to administer this legislation.
There is also going to be difficulty in satisfying that tribunal that a man is permanently unemployable. The result will be that applications will be turned down just as they were under the Pension Act. There is no assurance that the class for whom tins legislation is intended will get the compensation provided under this legislation.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, because of the inadequacy of the compensation, because of the difficulty in interpreting the measure, because of the fact that it is to be administered, not by an independent tribunal, but by a body under the minister's control, I contend that it will not satisfy the class of persons for whom it is intended, and therefore should not be accepted by the house as satisfactory.

This debate
has been most interesting. I feel that it is well that every member should contribute his opinion before this bill is sent to the committee, and that is why I am on my feet at the present moment. This is a very important bill, and if we reserve our criticism now we would not be giving to the members of the committee the assistance which they certainly are seeking.
I was delighted with the address of the hon. member for North York (Mr. Lennox) on this bill this afternoon. Himself a returned soldier, he spoke as a man familiar with the life and point of view of the soldier as only one who knows them intimately can. I thought when I heard the hon. member for North \ ork analyse this bill that the remarks made by the Minister of Pensions (Mr. King, Kootenay) on March 4th last deserved more consideration than I gave them at the time, In introducing the bill on that day the minister stated that there was an outstanding need in the lives of our veterans not provided foi under present legislation. I could not help but note the contrast between the words of the minister and the diatribes-shall I call them?-that we have heard against this bill to-night.
The object of the Board of Pension Commissioners, says the Minister of Pensions, is

Allowances to War Veterans
to take care of the veterans whose disabilities are attributable to war service, and the present bill, he says, is to provide for aged and unemployable veterans whose physical condition may not be attributable to war service. I should like the house to note exactly what is the object of this bill. It is for the relief of veterans who are aged and unemployable. The minister called that a major problem. He said:
This is the major problem that confronts the returned soldier.
In order to prove to the house that he was sincere, in order to show that this was a major measure for the benefit of the returned soldiers, he told us of the steps that he took in order to bring down a bill that would meet with the unanimous support of the house. ^ He told us that he had appointed a committee from his department and an officer of the soldier settlement board, who devoted their whole time to a study of this question.
I would also like the house to note the method whereby this bill proposes to ameliorate the condition of the returned soldiers. The minister says that he took special pains to ascertain the feeling of the returned soldiers of Canada, and that he is now presenting this bill as representing the united desire of every post of the legion throughout Canada. Surely in view of the number of letters t-hat have been received from every part of Canada, from even the paost remote! districts, by every member of the house during the last seven days, the minister cannot say that this bill represents the wishes of the great body of returned soldiers.
The minister also said that he had come to the conclusion that the situation he found was one to *be dealt with entirely apart from pension legislation. In what respect should it be dealt with apart from pension legislation? The minister cannot seriously state that this bill is a response to the demand of the soldiers who are seeking relief under the Pension Act. The minister dwells upon the aged and permanently unemployable, but what about the great number of returned soldiers who entered t'he theatre of war between 18 and 25, and 35 and 45 years, who are neither aged nor permanently unemployable, and who are not benefiting under the Pension Act? I contend that the time is long past when relief should have been brought down for those gallant boys who fought for us overseas.
I was very much impressed by the figures presented to the house to-day by the hon. member for North York. The Minister of Pensions, before concluding his remarks upon
this bill the other evening, referring to this wonderful measure which was going to be such a panacea for all the troubles of the returned soldiers, uttered these words:
If this bill is passed Canada will be a pioneer in enacting legislation of this character.
God forbid! I say God forbid that the genius of our country should be so blind or purblind as not to see the responsibility placed upon it. The hon. member for North York (Mr. Lennox), referring to the United States, mentioned that in eighteen months 213,000 casualties were suffered of which 187,000 received pensions. What does that mean to anyone who knows something about figures?
It means this, Mr. Speaker, that 88 per cent of those casualties are pensioned to-day. Canada prides herself upon the steps taken to ameliorate the conditions of her returned men, but what do we find? In four years the casualties among Canadian soldiers were 215,000. One hundred and fifty thousand Canadian soldiers returned to Canada; 61,000 died in foreign fields, and of the 150,000 casualties that were not fatal 28 per cent are receiving pensions. Is that something to be proud of? No, Mr. Speaker. We are all here pledged to give our best help towards putting into force some measure that will enable the great body of veterans to secure relief from their present condition. The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Cantley) quoted the Minister of Pensions and National Health , as saying that this was the only legislation to be brought before the house this year, the only form of relief which we were extending to returned soldiers-a relief which is only partial because it deals with but a small section of returned soldiers, namely the aged and unemployed, and the minister replied that it was not so. But I have in Hansard, under my hand, the very questions propounded on March 4 relative to that, the reason for the inquiries being that members on this side of the house are anxious that legislation be put in force this year to meet the requirements of returned soldiers who are not benefiting under the act. This is what I find:
Mr. Clark:	Is this the major matter to be
brought before that committee?
Mr. King (Kootenay):	I should say it was.
Mr. Clark: What other matters are to come before the committee?
Mr. King (Kootenay):	All matters which
have been before the house and matters which the legion and other soldier bodies may bring forward.
Mr. Clark: Is there any other specific matter to be referred to this special committee?
Mr. King (Kootenay):	You mean a government bill?
Mr. Clark:	Yes.
Mr. King (Kootenay):	No.

Allowances to War Veterans
That, Mr. Speaker, convinces us that this bill as it now stands is not meeting the requirements of those who seek relief. I do not wish at this time to take up the time of the house with the large number of letters which we receive from returned soldiers all over the country, but I have a letter here from New Brunswick, sent to me the day after I spoke in the house on the returned soldier question, and I have another from British Columbia which I do think indicates that the time has come when an independent commission divorced from politics and departmental influence must look after the returned soldier situation. As long as we have such a grave question tinged with a political aspect we cannot hope to solve the problem over which we have been quibbling for the last three or four years. We must have an independent commission. Here is a letter from a returned soldier that should enlighten every member in this house as to the importance of deciding now and once and for all the question: Are we capable, or are we not, of dealing with the problem of the returned soldier? Before I read it Mr. Speaker, I wish to add my tribute to the pension board. I have found them ever courteous, ever obliging, ever anxious to explain why this or that man is not getting the pension which in our heart of hearts we know he is entitled to. I shall read only part of this letter. He writes to the department in Ottawa:
Replying to your letter of February 21st, I would like to point out to you once more that your attitude in regard to my disability does not seem fair. I would refer you to my record of pension. When I received my pension of $2.50 in 1918 I had a 20 per cent disability and I received 5 per cent of that.
I would like to know on what grounds a man receiving a disability of 20 per cent was only given 5 per cent of it. It would be interesting to know how that was arrived at. The letter continues:
Furthermore, in 1919 I was reboarded by Dr. Wrench of Hazelton, and he found no pensionable disability.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, the doctor said "You have no pensionable disability," and the pension was cut off. Then the man continues :
I was reboarded about five years ago and was found to have a 50 per cent disability for which I receive 5 per cent, or $7.50 and my wife $2.50 making a total of $10 per month.
Then he said to the board:
I will againt remind you, I enlisted in 1915, and until I went overseas in 1917 I had only been on sick parade once. I was given the same examination as the other men and passed A-l for overseas duty. When our regiment landed IMr. Brady.]
in England from the hot boat and train we were put in tents with only the one blanket we had with us, and as the weather was very cold and frosty, it is a wonder any of us came back. I was boarded again in England and was sent from the work battalion at Perfleet to the infantry at Seaford. So taking it all into consideration it don't seem I am getting a square deal.
His trouble has been bronchitis and asthma, and 'he has had other troubles which prevent him from earning his living. In other words, last November that man was stricken down with a complex trouble, which included asthma, bronchitis and pneumonia, and to-day is not able to do the work Which he would have been able to do had he not been so stricken down.
Why should we not show ourselves a little more constructive in dealing with this major problem? Great memories, sir, demand great responses, and I do think we are not doing all that we should do for these men. We remember the days of the war when every bell in every steeple clashed and clanged when our men went overseas; we remember that our cities were illuminated for every victory recorded by the sons of Canada; we remember that in every temple and every church throughout the country, congregations knelt in silent prayer for the return of those men. So I wonder to-day, Mr. Speaker, why such a bill as the one before us now should be presented to this house and why we should be told it is solving the problem of the returned soldier, when thousands of men will not benefit by it. We want to see something done this session for the returned soldiers; we demand that something be done. These men gave everything they possessed; they gave all that man could give. Why, then, should a bill such as this be placed before us? I know, Mr. Speaker, that many men throughout Canada to-day would receive full compensation under our pension board if they did not have to appeal to that tribunal through the medium of some Liberal doctor. I know that and have proof of it.
That is most unfair. The doctors throughout the country are Liberal and Conservative. I think my hon. friend is very unfair to make that statement.

I can assure the minister that I meant just what I said. I felt that I should speak on this subject before the bill went to committee, because there are certain sections of the bill which are nothing less than childish, Tell me, Mr. Speaker, must a soldier wait until he is permanently disabled and not able to work in order to get this little old age pension of $20 per month? There are many soldiers

Allowances to War Veterans
throughout Canada who are crippled but who are working get a few dollars in order to keep the pot boiling. Must they wait until they are permanently disabled before they get any assistance? And then think of this wonderful gift that we are giving these soldiers; when a poor returned man is laid up and sent to the hospital, under this bill the little pension will cease.

No, no; let me correct my hon. friend, because that statement has been made before. It has been said that a pensioner going to a hospital would have his allowance under this bill cut off. The moment a pensioner goes to hospital he is put on pay and allowances, and if he is a .man with a wife and three children he will receive $125 per month. Let us be fair and not get confused.

Just to clear up the matter I should like to ask a question, with my hon. friends permission. The minister says a man with a wife and three children would get $125 per month, but the bill distinctly states that this allowance will be cut off. The other day the minister said that this is not part of the Pension Act, so how under those circumstances can the man receive pay and allowances?

I think that is a proper question, and I will try to explain. My hon. friend across the way (Mr. Brady) said that a pensioner going to the hospital would under this measure have his pension discontinued. This is not a pension; this is an allowance.
He used the wrong word; he meant "beneficiary".

This bill has
nothing to do with what we consider as a pension for war disability.
Therefore he would not get pay and allowances under this act?
No, he would not.
Then my hon. friend was correct.
No he was not; he did not use the right words.

So to-day, Mr. Speaker, we are placing the returned soldier outside the realm of equity; we are classing him with men who become decrepit through old age and the ordinary disabilities of life. I say that equity demands that the returned soldier be placed not under a bill such as this but under the Pension Act, to the benefits of which he is justly entitled. That is where I
think this bill does not meet the difficulty which now exists. Why did the minister segregate these veterans away from the pension act; why not extend the scope of that act to these men? They are entitled to a pension larger than the amount they will receive under this act by way of allowance.
A grave error was committed, Mr. Speaker, in not allying and associating the widow and children with the returned soldier. That is a matter of vast importance. There are many women to-day struggling against the most terrific odds to hold body and soul together, and they are ignored by the provisions of this bill. Far be it from me, Mr. Speaker, to do anything which would interfere with legislation to help the soldier body, but after listening to this debate and conscientiously endeavouring to understand the bill, I say that it does not meet the requirements of the soldier despite the fact that the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. King) has stated that he took a soldier and appointed a commission, and then presents this bill as representing the wishes of the returned soldiers.
Many dark clouds are overshadowing the evening of the returned soldier's day; many are waiting who cannot express what they feel regarding their diseases and nervous disorders which were the inevitable result of going to war. Since the returned soldier in the backwoods of British Columbia has no means of speaking his mind, since he holds in his heart the troubles of himself and his dependents caused by the limitations of the pension board, since he is not here to try to interpret his wishes, then it is my duty to plead his cause to the members of this house. I hope that this bill will emerge from the committee so perfect an instrument for the well being of the soldiers that no soldier will ever fear hereafter that justice will not be done unto him.

Mr. Speaker, I intend to take up but a few minutes of the time of the house. I did not intend to speak to-night, but the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Brady) has said that every member should express his thoughts. I had intended to speak the other evening in support of the resolution proposed by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. McGibbon) as amended by the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Ernst), but I cannot afford myself that opportunity to-night.
I am not going to criticize the government, but desire only to make a few remarks in the hope that something may come out of them. Many splendid speeches have been delivered in this house in connection with soldier problems, particularly in the debate upon the

Allowances to War Veterans

present bill and upon the resolution proposed the other night. Practically everyone who has spoken has demanded a wider interpretation of the Pension Act and I believe that that is the feeling of Canada as a whole. The government need have no fear from a generous treatment of the soldier. Governments do make mistakes, and I am satisfied that this government has made one in not accepting the resolution proposed by the hon. member for Muskoka. Had it accepted that resolution everything would have been satisfactory and much of the time of the house would have been saved. We have spent three or four days discussing this question; I do not say that that time has been wasted, but we would have accomplished as much had we accepted the resolution proposed by the hon. member for Muskoka.
I believe that this bill should be supported, with one exception, and that is with respect to the personnel of the committee which is to administer the act. I think both the bill and the proposed resolution should be sent to the committee with instructions to give the returned soldier a fair deal.
It is before the committee.

It is supposed to be. The hon. member is always butting in out of turn. The ministers are in the house to correct me if I am wrong; it is not his place to do that. He belongs over there, anyhow.
I think the country would be satisfied, and I think the returned soldiers would be satisfied with this bill, with that one exception-the personnel of the committee. My advice 10 the house is that that be eliminated.
Is the house ready for the question?
Carried.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. H. KING (Minister of Pensions and National Health):
speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I have a moment or two in which to close the debate?
The hon. minister may speak now if he so desires, but if he does so he will close the debate.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the present debate the principles of this measure are under consideration, and as I see it there are two principles involved; one is aid to be given to veterans, and the other is the method by which that aid is to be dispensed. Those who are to receive aid are men of the age of sixty-five; if they are not sixty-five years of age

they may receive aid but only upon the decision of a committee which is political in its character.
No.
It must be political because the members of the committee are employees of the government.
The government represents the people.

Of course the government represents the people, but it is political, and I am using the word "political" in its proper sense. The lessening of that age sixty-five will depend entirely on the attitude of the committee, which committee, as the minister very properly said the other day, is really under the control of the government. There is an appeal to him, and he represents a political party which in the very nature of things must be so. I protest. There should be some other tribunal which woidd be independent and free from political bias or prejudice, a tribunal incapable of being influenced by circumstances or, shall we say, by the influence of those who control or are interested in the control of votes. I make that statement to the minister quite frankly and I trust the government will see to it that the tribunal which will ultimately determine whether a man under the age of sixty-five is to receive the benefits of this measure is one free from politics and political control or supervision.
It necessarily follows that the man of sixty-five years of age, to receive the benefits of this measure, must have been fifty years of age when he went to the war, as it is something less than fifteen years since the most of these men -left for the war. Obviously the men in that category would be very limited in number, but the power that is given to this committee, responsible to the government, is to deal with the greatest number of cases, namely, those who were under fifty years when they went to the war. That means practically all or at least 90 per cent as a minimum. The minister thinks it is less than 90 per cent. Well, if it is less than 90 per cent, my observation is that the number who went to the war at fifty years of age or thereabouts, would not be more than 10 or 12 per cent of the total. Originally they were not allowed to enlist at fifty, as my hon. friend observes, but some of them managed to enlist by understating their age on account of a desire to serve their country and sometimes because they were in battalions in which they were permitted to serve even though their

Allowances to War Veterans

age was in excess of the age usually given as a maximum for enlistment. 1 hat principle of the measure is one that, I think, when the bill goes to committee, should be a matter that the government will see is remedied. I have no right to make any suggestion as to the character of the tribunal that should make this determination, but essentially I think it calls for the exercise of the veiy highest qualities of a judge. Upon this tribunal we confer the power of investigation under the Inquiries Act. It therefore contemplates the right to acquire knowledge and proof of the facts and to exercise judgment. I submit that that judgment should be a judicial determination of a question, on the evidence submitted. When a case has been made out that comes within the principle laid down by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Anderson) this afternoon, where a man under sixty-five, for instance, forty-five or forty or less, has, by reason of the circumstances to which attention has been directed, so suffered from physical deterioration that he is in the same condition as though he had reached the age of sixty-five, a decision should be given on the evidence as a judicial act and not otherwise. That 'being so, it does not appear that a tribunal of the kind provided by the bill can render that impartial judgment which is so essential in a matter of this nature if we are to expect to secure the support of an enlightened public opinion.
The second principle of the measure, that is the question as to the amount to be paid, and the principles under which the amount is to be received, is a matter of detail that can well be considered by the committee, and with respoct to Which I am not at the moment concerned, beyond saying this:	That principle of the measure involves the acceptance of a view to which, as I explained the other day on the first reading of the resolution, I am not prepared to agree. I am not going to repeat What I said on that occasion, except to say that the measure of benefit and the terms under which the benefit is to be conferred involve the acceptance of a condition which the applicant should not be compelled to put forward before he is the recipient of the benefit. That is, no man who has become a wreck on account of service for his country should be compelled to put forward his impoverished condition financially as a reason for receiving a benefit from the state. If we put forward his physical condition as the basis of his claim for benefits, then he is entitled to a pension and if he receives a pension, his dependents would, in the event of his death, also be entitled to
benefits. Under those circumstances I think the measure cannot be said to meet the difficulties to which attention has so often been directed I desire only to point out that the twe principles upon which the measure rests are in my judgment, principles that are not consonant with the exercise of a sound judgment and a fair attitude of mind on the part ol the country towards those who are no longer fit to discharge the ordinary duties of life because of the service they rendered their country in the war. I will not say more than that because the committee, if the government so desire, they having control, may be able to make it perfectly clear that that principle is one that is unsound, and that a committee set up by a government department shall not be the determining factor as to whether or not an applicant is entitled to the benefits under the measure.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. H. KING (Minister of Pensions and National Health):
speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I propose to take only a few moments in dealing with the discussion which has taken place this afternoon. On the introduction of the bill the other day I briefly set forth the principles contained in the legislation. It was, I think, explained that the legislation proposed by this bill was not intended to be considered in the same manner as ordinary pension legislation that had been heretofore brought before parliament. I explained1 at the time that our pension legislation was -built upon certain principles which were well defined and well known. As a parliament we know-and I think the government have been confirmed in their position'-that if [those principles are to be disturbed-and from time to time proposals have been made that they should be- the matter should be referred to a special committee of file house where the proposals might be considered and analyzed >as to what, the results might be and the house might be so advised through the knowledge obtained by the committee.
There have been many committees of parliament which have considered pension matters. In 1923 there was a special committee which dealt with the recommendations of a royal' commission, and amendtoients were made to the Pension Act. The federal appeal board, was brought into being. The federal appeal board was criticized this afternoon by the hon. member for No-rth York (Mr. Lennox), but. I do not 'think he had the data before him. His statement, at least, did not cover the full activities of the appeal board. In the annual report there will be found a statement made by the federal appeal board indicating the.

Allowances to War Veterans
work that was done, the number of appeals that have 'been under review and1 the number that have 'been ruled upon by them. This is all set out on page 65 of the report. I am not going to delay in making reply, but I would ask hon. members-because my hon. friend's statement has again been referred to this evening-to check that statement and ascertain the facts as to the results and what the federal appeal board has been doing.
Since the war, various official soldier bodies in Canada have been representing to the people and to our parliamentary committees their desires and wishes and what they thought was due to the soldiers. First we had the Great War Veterans' Association, a large organization that sprang up all over Canada, a new organization. Then we had the older organization of the Army and Navy Veterans which is still in existence. Then under the leadership of Earl Haig we had an empire organization of which the Canadian soldiers became a part, it being now known as the Canadian Legion. To-day reference was made to General Currie and his letter. General Currie was appointed president of the legion in June, 1928, in St. John, after a special committee of the house had dealt with the Pension Act of that year. General Currie remained president of that organization until November of last year. Unfortunately during the period of his presidency he was not able, on account of illn&ss, to give that attention which he would otherwise have given to the affairs of the legion and the soldiers o'f Canada. It is true that in November of last year he wrote a letter to the legion suggesting that he thought that further legislation should be brought diown, and that the returned men should not be left without consideration.
And that the Pension Act should be revised.

And that the Pension A at should be revised. It was suggested this afternoon that the Prime Minister's statement in London was a follow-up of General Currie's letter. Well, I do not know. I was in Vancouver before the meeting of the legion and 'before the publication of General Currie's letter in November, and I heard the Prime Minister make practically the same statement in Vancouver that he made in London a few weeks ago. Why did the Prime Minister deal with the subject at that time?
An election was coming on.
Not at all.

Certainly.
I Mr. J. H. King.]

Not at all. Just be reasonable, and we will find out. As I said a few moments ago, under the leadership of Earl Haig, the empire soldier body was formed, and the Canadian legion came into being. They held their first meeting, I believe, in Port Anthur or Fort William in 1927, and passed many resolutions; I think 135 of them were presented to me as minister in January and February of that year. I met the officers of the legion and said to them frankly, "There are many matters here of great importance to you and to the country. This is a new parliament, and you come in the midst of the session and expect us to deal with all these matters. I would suggest to you that you leave them with us, and I will circularize every member of parliament, sending a copy of your resolutions to them, and in the interval these matters that you have in mind may be considered and canvassed by the members of parliament in their own districts." That course was followed. I promised, in addition, that the government would appoint a special committee in 1928 before which these matters could be brought and there be fully discussed. The legion accepted that proposal, and we had our committee of 1928.
Then we had the legion's second meeting in St. John in June, 1928, just at the close of the session, after .the committee had reported to parliament, and we know what were the results of that meeting of the legion. The matters that were dealt with and passed by the committee were considered by the legion, and were well received. This year the legion met in Regina in November. I was invited to attend, and would like to have attended. Other members of this house, some of them returned soldiers and others who were not, were also invited to attend. For what purpose? In order that there might be a further review of the soldier field, and that the legion might through their officers and membership again present to parliament and to the people what they thought would be a further advance in returned soldier legislation. It was understood, I think, by all members of this parliament, at least it was understood in government circles, that in all probability there would come out of the meeting of the legion this year recommendations which would of necessity have to be referred to a special committee of this house.
In addition, as I stated the other day, there was the resolution passed by the parliamentary committee of 1928, setting forth that certain conditions among the returned soldiers were

Allowances to War Veterans
not being taken care of under the pension legislation, and that other means should be em-ployed to take care of the burnt-out or prematurely old men.
Has the minister any figures to show what proportion of the entire number of returned soldiers belong to the legion? I have not myself, but I thought perhaps the minister would have.

My information from legion headquarters is that between seventy-five and eighty thousand returned men are members of that organization.
Knowing the problem as we know it from day to day, there is no doubt that the care of our soldiery is one of the most difficult departments to administer. In the matter of admission to our hospitals, and in their management, a certain latitude has been allowed to the department by the legislation which has built it up. The governor in council has been given, by legislation, certain liberties and certain opportunities to serve in the care of our soldiers, but we have had on our doorstep men who had served, and served well, but had no apparent pensionable disability, and who were becoming old and finding it difficult to get employment. They were requiring some form of assistance.
The idea of a pension to the aged soldier is not new in this house. It is being criticised now by our friends opposite, but I remember very well that in 1926 when I introduced the Old Age Pension Act there were suggestions then from our friends opposite that we should insert in that act a clause that would make its provisions applicable to the soldier at the age of sixty-five. We took exception to that because we were dealing with a civilian matter, and a matter that was new to the people of Canada. From our experience and our investigation of this problem we know that this year, next year, the year after, and so on, there will be soldiers reaching the age of sixty-five, and we can estimate very fairly what the cost to this country will be as regards those men. The uncertain quantity is the men who have not reached the age of sixty-five but who from illness or other causes are to-day found to be unemployable on account of disability. We have concluded that there is no body of men in Canada who can so well judge and make an accurate survey of that situation as the officers of the Department of Pensions and National Health. We have some 1,800 employees engaged in this work from day to day. We are dealing with some 3,500 soldiers who are going in and out of our hospitals from day to day. We are dealing
in the winter season with from 3,000 to 3,200 people who are receiving relief from day to day. I can understand my hon. friends taking exception to the minister having the final say in these matters, but, Mr. Speaker, is it not better for the people of this country, is it not better for the opposition in this parliament to have the minister take the responsibility, meet parliament each year, give an account of his administration and face the consequences, than to get behind a commission, which has been the policy hitherto followed in dealing with soldier matters? I think myself that our troubles are largely due to the fact that both parties in parliament have not been prepared to face the issue and bring down legislation, legislation which the soldiers probably should have had, and should have at this time. Instead we have sheltered ourselves behind commissions, and it is probably due to that that we have not had the best results. After all, the minister each year is subject to the criticism of the opposition and of those who are opposing the government, and the ministry must in the end, as I have done in the last few days, as far as this house and the country are concerned, accept the responsibility of the presumably independent board which will deal with these matters.
Does the minister think it would be better to have a departmental committee administering pensions rather than the pension commissioners?

No, I have not said that. I do say that all along we have been most anxious to keep this matter out of politics and in attempting to do that we probably have not faced our responsibility as we should have. But in this matter-because after all we are dealing with only one phase, and it is not, and should not be considered, a phase of the present Pension Act-we are bringing in a new piece of legislation to deal with special conditions which have arisen during the years since the war. If we had not brought in this legislation, then I am satisfied we would have had to come before parliament and in our estimates ask for large sums of money this year in order that we might establish homes where the aged soldier might have care and treatment. That matter will be discussed no doubt in committee. The judgment of the departmental committee may be found wrong, but it is the experience of those engaged in social work to-day that it is better not to break up the home, but rather to try to maintain it by giving sufficient allowances so that the old man and his wife may continue to live together, and

Allowances to War Veterans
the man who happens to be single at the age of sixty-five may have the opportunity to live with his relatives or friends. We had the alternative of establishing homes or of increasing our relief to the veterans. I think, Mr. Speaker, when the committee have had an opportunity of calling before it those officers who have carefully studied this problem it will endorse this bill. So far as I am personally concerned, I am not anxious'about the administration. I know that the soldiers themselves do not wish this bill to be mixed up with pension matters, they do not wish it to be referred to and administered by the pension board or the appeal board. It may be better to build up another board, but I do not think it is necessary, and I think it will be shown in the committee that the departmental officers, who are situated not only in Ottawa but in every large centre throughout the Dominion, will be able to deal with this bill and its administration better than any body that can be set up in the way of a committee or a commission.
May I ask the hon. minister a question?
Yes.
I thought he said just now that we have a body of men in every part of Canada to deal with the matter.
Yes, we have.
Does that mean that the question whether men under sixty-five shall receive these benefits will be determined in each province by a committee in that province?
No, it will be done just as a matter of administration day by day.
By the officials of the department in that province?
Yes.
That is absolutely ghastly.
That is not in the bill.

We will use the machinery that we have, just as that machinery to-day is being used under the chief medical officer, who admits patients to hospitals in Vancouver, Edmonton, Fort William and other centres.

Certainly it is not in the bill. The bill contemplates only one committee. Now the minister says there will be a committee in each province.
TMr. J. H. King.]

No, there is a
misunderstanding. We will have a departmental committee which will be composed as set out in the bill, but that committee will utilize the machinery available in every province. A few day's ago the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Clark) suggested that we should utilize the machinery of the provincial old age pension boards. I should like to say so far as that is concerned that the machinery available to the Department of Pensions and National Health, is, I think, better organized and has greater facilities than the provincial old age pension boards that he spoke of.

The minister said
that the men do not wish this legislation mixed up with the pension board. Did they give any reasons why they would prefer it this way rather than under the pension board?

Yes. I might
say for the information of the house that in developing this legislation we have gone pretty far afield to inquire as to these and other proposals that I have suggested, and we have come in contact with the soldier organizations and outstanding men who have had the soldiers' interests at heart throughout the Dominion. We have also gone to the various provincial departments for information, and in our conversations they said they feared that this bill might be considered a pension matter, and they were of the opinion that it should be kept free and distinct from the ordinary pension matters and pension legislation in its administration. I think I may confirm that by reading what Colonel LaFleche said recently. This is quoted from the Ottawa Journal of March 5:
Complete approval of the principle of the war veterans' allowance bill was expressed by Colonel LaFleche.
"This bill must not deprive any war veteran of a disability pension," he stated. "I feel assured, however, that this will not be likely to occur, for the fact that the administration of the War Veterans' Allowance Act .... is to be by a committee specially appointed for the purpose."

That is merely a
suggestion, not a reason. Was any reason given why the pension board should not administer this as a separate piece of legislation?

The pension board themselves said they thought it would be a mistake to ask them to administer this bill as it was outside their jurisdiction and there should not be a conflict between the two. Reference has been made to my having

Companies Act Amendment
stated the other night that this was the measure the government had brought down- had initiated; that is what I meant. At that time it was understood there was to be a special committee and that the usual procedure would be followed, that resolutions moved by my hon. friends opposite would be referred to that committee just as this bill will be referred to it. We are hopeful that out of that committee-and it is a very excellent one-wiH come legislation which the government and parliament will endorse, legislation which will be for the benefit and advantage of the soldiers.
I do not think, Mr. Speaker, that I should delay the house at any greater length. We have given much thought and study to the measure. We think it will serve a very useful purpose in solving this great problem. If it is improved in committee, so much the better, but I think when the whole situation is canvassed this bill will be endorsed by the committee and will be returned to the house for endorsation.
Do I understand that this bill is intended primarily to take care of deferred disability cases?

No, this bill will
not take care of any case which has the right to go to the Board of Pension Commissioners and get a pension, with the exception of the case that gets a small pension varying from 5 to 15 per cent.
Fourteen per cent.
Fourteen per cent, yes. In that case the bill would supplement the Pension Act.
Up to the maximum.

Up to the maximum, yes.
